subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 22-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus is brought to the emergency department with vomiting, abdominal pain, and Kussmaul respirations. Laboratory studies show glucose 520 mg/dL, arterial pH 7.08, and markedly elevated serum beta-hydroxybutyrate. Her hepatic fatty acid synthesis is very low, while fatty acid oxidation and ketogenesis are increased.
question: Which of the following best explains the decreased activity of hepatic acetyl-CoA carboxylase in this patient?
explanation_correct: In diabetic ketoacidosis, insulin deficiency and glucagon excess raise hepatic cAMP, which activates protein kinase A and inactivates acetyl-CoA carboxylase by phosphorylation. The resulting fall in malonyl-CoA relieves inhibition of carnitine palmitoyltransferase I, so long-chain fatty acids enter mitochondria, undergo beta-oxidation, and are converted to ketone bodies.

explanation_incorrect.A: Citrate allosterically activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase, so an increase would stimulate rather than inhibit fatty acid synthesis.
explanation_incorrect.B: Insulin activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase and promotes fatty acid synthesis, and this patient is insulin deficient.
explanation_incorrect.C: Malonyl-CoA is the product of the reaction; it inhibits carnitine palmitoyltransferase I rather than acetyl-CoA carboxylase.
explanation_incorrect.E: A decrease in cAMP would activate acetyl-CoA carboxylase, but hepatic cAMP is increased in ketoacidosis.

educationalObjective: Glucagon acting through cAMP inactivates acetyl-CoA carboxylase, lowering malonyl-CoA and promoting beta-oxidation and ketogenesis.
